summary: Iconic bottom-dwelling groundfish targeted on a short, tightly controlled recreational season, with different windows and limits depending on whether you fish the Gulf side (NB, PEI, and the Northumberland Strait shore of NS) or the Atlantic/Bay of Fundy side of Nova Scotia.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*) are heavy-bodied bottom fish, brown to greenish-grey on the back and flanks fading to a pale belly, with small smooth scales. Identify them by the single chin barbel, three rounded dorsal fins, two anal fins, and a distinct pale, curved lateral line running the length of the body. They can live 25 years and reach over 2 m and 90+ kg in the open ocean, though recreationally caught fish in this region are almost always much smaller — commonly in the 40–70 cm range.

Cod are opportunistic bottom feeders, eating capelin, herring, sand eels, crab, shrimp, and other groundfish, which is why bottom rigs baited with cut bait or squid, and shiny diamond jigs worked near bottom, both work. They relate strongly to structure and bottom contour: reefs, drop-offs, wharves, and current edges over hard bottom in 30–300+ ft of water.

The stock picture matters here. Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence cod has been in the Critical Zone of DFO's Precautionary Approach framework for decades, with spawning stock biomass down from roughly 320,000 tonnes in the 1950s to about 12,000 tonnes by 2023 — a collapse largely tied to very high natural mortality (60–70% of gulf cod die before age 5, much of it attributed to grey seal predation) rather than fishing alone. This is why both DFO regions run the recreational fishery on short, tightly bounded windows rather than an open season.

sections.heading: Two Different Rulebooks — Which One Applies to You
sections.body_md:
This is the single most important thing to understand before you go: **New Brunswick, PEI, and the Nova Scotia side of the Northumberland Strait / Gulf of St. Lawrence fall under DFO Gulf Region rules.** The Nova Scotia Atlantic coast (Halifax and points east/west), the Bay of Fundy shore, and the Scotian Shelf fall under **DFO Maritimes Region rules** — a separate management framework with its own season windows and bag limits.

Practically: if you're fishing from a wharf in Shediac, Cocagne, or Miramichi Bay (NB), anywhere around PEI, or the NS shore facing the Northumberland Strait (e.g., Pictou, Antigonish, Cape Breton's Gulf side), you're under **Gulf Region** rules. If you're fishing Halifax Harbour, the South Shore, the Bay of Fundy (Saint John side included), or the NS Atlantic coast east to Cape North, you're under **Maritimes Region** rules. See the Regulations section below — the season dates and bag limits genuinely differ.

sources.label: DFO Gulf Region — Recreational Groundfish Fishery, Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence
DFO Maritimes Region — Groundfish (Recreational Fisheries)

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md:
### Gulf Region (NB, PEI, NS Northumberland Strait side)
Per DFO Gulf Region's 2026 notice (issued April 14, 2026), the general recreational groundfish season within 50 m of the coastline runs **April 15 to October 1**. Cod and white hake specifically may only be *retained* during a shorter access window inside that season:
- **New Brunswick:** sunrise to sunset, **July 16 – August 21, 2026**
- **Nova Scotia (Gulf/Strait shore) and PEI:** sunrise to sunset, **August 1 – September 5, 2026**

Outside those cod/white hake windows you can still fish for other groundfish under the general season, but cod must be released.

### Maritimes Region (NS Atlantic coast, Bay of Fundy, Scotian Shelf)
DFO Maritimes Region splits the coast into two zones with different windows (page last updated 2023-07-31 — confirm current-year dates against the Maritimes Orders Registry before you go, noted below):
- **Halifax Harbour and west** (includes the Bay of Fundy shore): open Feb 1 – Dec 31 generally, but cod **retention** only permitted from the **3rd Saturday in June through Labour Day**.
- **Hartlen Point eastward to Cape North** (including the Bras d'Or lakes): open **3rd Saturday in June through Labour Day**.

### Time of Day / Conditions
No DFO-mandated time-of-day restriction beyond the sunrise-to-sunset retention window in the Gulf region. Locally, anglers report better action around tide changes and when bait (herring, mackerel, capelin) is thick in the area — fish where the bait and bottom structure are, not just where it's convenient.

sources.label: DFO Gulf Region — Recreational Groundfish Fishery, Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence (Notice, April 14, 2026)
DFO Maritimes Region — Groundfish (Recreational Fisheries)

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
Cod relate to hard bottom, drop-offs, and current — wharves and breakwaters over deep water, reefs, and offshore ledges all hold fish.

**New Brunswick (Gulf side):** Grand Manan wharves are consistently reported to produce cod alongside pollock, mackerel, and sculpin — note Grand Manan itself sits in the Bay of Fundy so double check which regional rules apply to the exact spot you fish there. Wharf and pier fishing around Miramichi Bay and the Northumberland Strait shore is a common local pattern for groundfish generally.

**PEI:** North Lake Harbour, on the eastern tip of the Island near East Point, is the hub for charter boats working deep water off East Point — trips there target bluefin tuna primarily but also fish for cod and mackerel along the way. Multiple charter operators (Ernie's Charter Fishing, PEI Tuna Charters, North Lake Charters) run out of this harbour.

**Nova Scotia (Atlantic side):** Local forum reports point to the Atlantic side generally producing cod wherever anglers can reach deep water (50+ ft) from shore, fishing hard on bottom with bait such as sandworms, crab, or cut fish. Cape Sable Island's Westhead Wharf was historically a shore-fishing cod spot, though longtime locals note catches there are far lighter than decades ago. The Bras d'Or Lakes (Cape Breton) are also called out as holding steady cod action by local anglers.

Treat all of the above as starting points, not guarantees — cod numbers in this region are a fraction of historical levels, and local, current information from wharf regulars or a charter captain beats any general guide.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod | Medium-heavy to heavy conventional or spinning rod, 6.5–7 ft — cod fishing means muscling fish and heavy jigs/weight off deep bottom. |
| Reel | Conventional or heavy spinning reel holding 200+ yards of 40–65 lb braid; braid's thin diameter and no-stretch feel matters a lot at depth. |
| Diamond jigs | 4–16 oz chrome/hammered diamond jigs depending on depth and current — heavier in deeper water or stronger current to stay in contact with bottom. |
| Bottom rig | Two-hook high-low rig or a single hook dropper loop above a bank/pyramid sinker sized to hold bottom (4–16 oz depending on depth/current). |
| Bait | Fresh cut mackerel, herring, squid strips, clam, or sandworms — cut bait fished hard on bottom is a proven producer. |
| Leader | 50–80 lb fluorocarbon or mono leader, 3–4 ft, tied to a barrel swivel above the jig or rig. |
| Extras | Long-nose pliers or a hook-out tool, a sturdy net or gaff (where retention is legal), and a descending device if fishing water deeper than about 20 m and planning to release fish (see Handling section). |

sources.label: CallOutdoors, How To Fish For Cod (Rig & Techniques)

sections.heading: Technique: Bottom Rig with Cut Bait
sections.body_md:
The simplest, most consistent producer for shore and boat anglers alike, especially over structure or drop-offs.

1. Rig a high-low (two-hook) rig or a single dropper-loop hook above enough weight (pyramid or bank sinker, 4–16 oz) to hold bottom in the current you're fishing.
2. Bait hooks with fresh cut mackerel, herring, or squid strips — fresh bait outfishes stale bait for cod by a wide margin.
3. Cast or drop the rig to bottom and let it sit; cod feed by scent and will find a stationary bait.
4. Keep light contact with the line — a few soft taps followed by steady weight is a cod picking up and moving off with the bait, not just mouthing it.
5. When you feel that steady pull, reel down to take up slack and set with a firm, steady lift — no need for a hard, fast hookset with circle-style bottom rigs.
6. Retrieve steadily; cod don't fight erratically like a pelagic species, but they're heavy and will bulldog on the way up, especially from real depth.

sources.label: CallOutdoors, How To Fish For Cod (Rig & Techniques)

sections.heading: Technique: Diamond Jig
sections.body_md:
Better for covering water and working structure or marked fish from a boat.

1. Drop a 4–16 oz chrome or hammered diamond jig straight to bottom, adjusting weight so the jig still reaches bottom and stays in reasonable contact with it given the current.
2. On contact, reel up a foot or two to keep the jig just off bottom and avoid constant snags.
3. Work it with sharp upward rod sweeps of 2–3 ft, letting it fall back on a controlled semi-slack line — the erratic fall is what triggers strikes, so don't rip it back down.
4. Vary cadence and drop speed through the day — sometimes a slower, more deliberate jig outfishes an aggressive one, and vice versa.
5. Adding a teaser fly or scented soft-plastic on a short dropper 2–3 ft above the jig can pick up extra fish, particularly when cod are keyed on smaller bait like sand eels.
6. Jigging works best with good bait presence (herring/mackerel schools nearby) and manageable current — in heavy current the jig won't fish correctly and bottom rigs will out-produce it.

sources.label: Hogy Lures, Offshore Jigging Cod | Haddock | Pollock
CallOutdoors, How To Fish For Cod (Rig & Techniques)

sections.heading: Handling & Release — Barotrauma Matters
sections.body_md:
Cod caught from any real depth suffer barotrauma as gas in the swim bladder expands on the way up, and this is the single biggest factor in whether a released fish survives.

- **Depth thresholds matter.** Research on Atlantic cod found a 50% probability of swim bladder rupture by about 13 m of capture depth, essentially 100% rupture by 19 m or deeper, and mortality rates over 40% for fish held at the surface after capture from 50 m or deeper.
- **If you're keeping your legal bag limit, this is moot** — dispatch and ice the fish promptly.
- **If you're releasing a fish** (because you're over your bag limit, it's outside the retention window, or it's simply not one you want): minimize fight time, minimize handling and surface exposure, and get the fish back down quickly. The same research found no mortality in cod that were caged and returned to capture depth for 72 hours afterward, versus much higher mortality when fish were simply released at the surface with an expanded, ruptured swim bladder and no way to resubmerge.
- **Use a descending device** for any fish caught deeper than roughly 20 m that you intend to release — a weighted clip or inverted hook that carries the fish back down before releasing it. This is standard best practice recommended across recreational groundfish/rockfish fisheries and directly supported by the cod-specific barotrauma research above.
- Avoid deep-hooking and gill damage where possible — a fish that's bleeding heavily is unlikely to survive release regardless of barotrauma treatment.

sources.label: ICES Journal of Marine Science, Dive to survive: effects of capture depth on barotrauma and post-release survival of Atlantic cod in recreational fisheries
NOAA Fisheries, Rockfish Barotrauma and Recompression

sections.heading: Conservation & Consumption Notes
sections.body_md:
Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence cod has sat in the Critical Zone of DFO's Precautionary Approach framework for decades, with spawning stock biomass around 12,000 tonnes as of 2023 — roughly 4% of its 1950s peak — and DFO's own assessments describe the longer-term outlook as dire with little prospect of recovery absent major ecosystem change, largely due to heavy natural mortality (grey seal predation on cod aged 5+) rather than fishing pressure alone. A formal rebuilding plan exists for cod in NAFO Divisions 4T and 4Vn.

Given that, the short, narrow retention windows and modest bag limits set by both DFO Gulf and Maritimes regions aren't arbitrary — they reflect a stock under real stress. Fish within your legal bag limit, handle any fish you release as carefully as described above, and treat a good day of cod fishing in this region as the exception, not the rule.

No consumption/mercury advisory specific to Atlantic cod was found for this region; cod is a standard, widely eaten whitefish with mild flavor and firm flakes — pan-fried, baked, or in chowder are all standard preparations.

sources.label: CBC News, Downward spiral for Atlantic cod continues in Gulf of St. Lawrence
DFO, Rebuilding plan: Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua) NAFO Divisions 4T and 4Vn

variants.name: Haddock
variants.how_to_tell: Haddock has a straight, dark (almost black) lateral line, versus cod's pale, curved lateral line — this is the fastest field check. Haddock also carries a distinct dark oval blotch ("the Devil's thumbprint") above and behind the pectoral fin that cod never has, and lacks cod's chin barbel entirely (cod's barbel is obvious and always present). Haddock's body is a cleaner silvery-grey without cod's mottled brown-to-greenish blotching, and its tail is slightly forked with a dark rear edge versus cod's more rounded/square tail.
variants.where_found: Deeper offshore banks and ledges, generally in the same grounds as cod but more associated with clean sand/gravel bottom; caught alongside cod on the Scotian Shelf and Bay of Fundy side of NS.
variants.notes: Haddock is zero-retention under the 2026 DFO Gulf Region notice — must be released immediately in NB, PEI, and the NS Northumberland Strait/Gulf shore, exactly like pollock, even during the open cod window. On the DFO Maritimes Region side (NS Atlantic coast, Bay of Fundy), haddock retention is permitted within the same aggregate groundfish bag limit as cod and pollock (10/day Halifax Harbour and west, 5/day Hartlen Point and east). Confusing a haddock for a cod on the Gulf side and keeping it is a real, avoidable violation — check the lateral line and thumbprint before it goes in the cooler.

variants.name: Pollock
variants.how_to_tell: Pollock has a forked tail (cod's is rounded/square), a protruding lower jaw that projects past the upper jaw (cod's upper jaw projects further), and a chin barbel that's tiny or absent versus cod's obvious barbel. Pollock's back runs olive-green to smoky black rather than cod's brown-to-greenish mottling, and its lateral line is straighter and less distinctly pale than cod's curved one.
variants.where_found: Same wharves, breakwaters, and offshore structure as cod region-wide; pollock also feed well up in the water column and even at the surface, unlike bottom-hugging cod.
variants.notes: Retention rules genuinely differ between the two species in the Gulf Region: pollock is zero-retention there in 2026 while cod has a short open window and a 5-fish sub-limit within the 15-fish groundfish aggregate. Mistaking a pollock for a legal cod (or vice versa) on the Gulf side has real consequences — check jaw, tail, and barbel before deciding what goes in the cooler.

variants.name: Atlantic Tomcod
variants.how_to_tell: Tomcod are a dwarf cod-family relative, not a juvenile Atlantic cod — the giveaway is size: tomcod max out around 15 cm (6 in), while even small recreationally-caught cod run 40+ cm. Both have three dorsal fins, two anal fins, and a chin barbel, so a small tomcod can superficially resemble a baby cod at a glance, but no genuinely juvenile Atlantic cod of that tiny size shows up on typical estuary or wharf gear in this region.
variants.where_found: Estuaries and river mouths (e.g. the Shubenacadie, NS) rather than the open coastal and offshore structure cod relate to.
variants.notes: No regulatory concern — both are legal to target where seasons allow — but worth knowing tomcod is its own species, not a undersized cod, if one turns up on flounder gear in an estuary.
